title: UP BOARD CLASS 5 — English | Clauses
description: Subject-wise test on Clauses (English) for UP BOARD CLASS 5. 50Q.
subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a clause?

options.explanation: A single word cannot be a clause because it lacks both a subject and a verb.

options.text: A group of words that makes complete sense on its own
options.explanation: This describes an independent clause, but not all clauses are independent.

options.text: A group of words that has a subject and a verb
options.explanation: This is the definition of a clause.

options.text: A group of words that describes a noun
options.explanation: This describes a phrase, not a clause.

questions.explanation: A clause is defined as a group of words that contains both a subject and a verb. It may or may not express a complete thought.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Identify the clause in the following sentence: 'The little bird sang sweetly.'

options.explanation: This is the subject, but it is not a complete clause.
This is the verb and a modifier, but it lacks a subject.
This contains both a subject and a verb, making it a clause.
This is an adverb, not a clause.

questions.explanation: A clause must contain both a subject and a verb. In this sentence, 'The little bird' is the subject and 'sang' is the verb. Therefore, 'The little bird sang' forms the clause.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Is 'running in the park' a clause?

options.text: Yes, because it describes an action.
options.explanation: Describing an action is not enough to make it a clause; it needs a subject.

options.text: No, because it does not have a subject.
options.explanation: This is correct; a clause must have a subject and a verb.

options.text: Yes, because it has a verb.
options.explanation: Having a verb is not enough; a clause also needs a subject.

options.text: No, because it is too short.
options.explanation: Length is not the determining factor for what constitutes a clause.

questions.explanation: For a group of words to be a clause, it must have both a subject and a verb. 'Running in the park' has a verb form ('running') but no explicit subject performing the action, making it a phrase, not a clause.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of these sentences has only one clause?

options.text: I like apples, and he likes bananas.
options.explanation: This sentence contains two clauses joined by 'and'.

options.text: When it rains, we stay indoors.
options.explanation: This sentence contains two clauses: one dependent and one independent.
This sentence has only one subject-verb pair, making it a single clause.

options.text: She sings well, but he dances better.
options.explanation: This sentence contains two clauses joined by 'but'.

questions.explanation: A sentence with only one subject-verb pair is considered a single clause. In 'My cat is sleeping,' 'My cat' is the subject and 'is sleeping' is the verb, forming one clause.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Complete the sentence with a suitable clause: 'I love to read books, _______.'

options.explanation: This is an adverbial phrase, not a clause.
This is a prepositional phrase, not a clause.
This is a phrase, not a clause, as it lacks a verb.

options.text: and my brother loves to draw
options.explanation: This adds a second clause with a subject ('my brother') and a verb ('loves to draw').

questions.explanation: The first part 'I love to read books' is a clause. To complete it with another clause, we need another subject-verb combination. 'My brother loves to draw' provides 'my brother' as the subject and 'loves to draw' as the verb, forming a second clause.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Read the sentence: 'She likes to sing, but he prefers to dance.' How many clauses are there in this sentence?

options.explanation: There are two subject-verb pairs, making it more than one clause.
The sentence contains two independent clauses joined by 'but'.
There are only two subject-verb pairs, not three.
The sentence clearly contains clauses.

questions.explanation: This sentence contains two distinct subject-verb pairs: 1) 'She likes to sing' (Subject: She, Verb: likes to sing) and 2) 'he prefers to dance' (Subject: he, Verb: prefers to dance). These are joined by the conjunction 'but,' indicating two clauses.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following options can stand alone as a complete sentence?

options.explanation: This is a dependent clause because it starts with 'while' and cannot stand alone.
This is a dependent clause because it starts with 'because' and cannot stand alone.
This has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete thought.
This is a dependent clause because it starts with 'if' and cannot stand alone.

questions.explanation: A group of words that can stand alone as a complete sentence is an independent clause. 'The children laughed loudly' has a subject ('The children') and a verb ('laughed loudly') and expresses a complete thought.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** 'The sun shines brightly' is a clause. **Reason (R):** It has a subject ('The sun') and a verb ('shines').

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: R is indeed the correct explanation for A.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: This is correct; A is true, and R explains why A is true.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: R is true; it correctly identifies the components of a clause.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: A is true; 'The sun shines brightly' is indeed a clause.

questions.explanation: The assertion is true because 'The sun shines brightly' contains a subject ('The sun') and a verb ('shines'). The reason correctly explains why it is a clause by identifying these two essential components.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following groups of words *cannot* be a clause on its own?

options.explanation: This is an independent clause; it can stand alone.
This is an independent clause; it has a subject and a verb and can stand alone.
This is a dependent clause because it starts with 'when' and cannot stand alone as a complete thought.
This is an independent clause; it can stand alone as a complete thought.

questions.explanation: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence is a dependent clause. 'When the bell rang' has a subject ('the bell') and a verb ('rang'), but the word 'When' makes it dependent, meaning it needs more information to form a complete thought.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Read the short passage: 'My dog loves to play. He chases the ball. When I throw it, he brings it back quickly.' How many clauses are there in the entire passage?

options.explanation: There are more than two clauses in the passage.
There are more than three clauses in the passage.
The passage contains four clauses: two independent and two that form a complex sentence.
There are not five distinct clauses in the passage.

questions.explanation: Let's break down the passage into clauses: 'My dog loves to play' is one clause, 'He chases the ball' is another, 'When I throw it' is a dependent clause, and 'he brings it back quickly' is an independent clause. So, there are four clauses in total.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a 'clause'?

options.explanation: A single word does not form a clause as it lacks both a subject and a verb.

options.text: A group of words that makes sense but does not have a subject and a verb
options.explanation: This describes a phrase, not a clause.

options.text: A group of words that has a subject and a verb
options.explanation: This is the correct definition of a clause.
A punctuation mark is not a clause.

questions.explanation: A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a verb.
questions.hint: A clause must have a subject and a verb to express a complete thought.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: In the sentence, 'The cat slept,' which part is the 'subject'?

options.explanation: Slept is the verb, not the subject.
The cat is the subject as it tells us who performed the action.
The is an article, not the subject.
Cat slept is the predicate, not the subject.

questions.explanation: The subject of a sentence tells us who or what the sentence is about.
questions.hint: The subject performs the action or is the topic of the sentence.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Look at the sentence: 'Birds sing beautifully.' Which group of words shows the 'action' in this sentence?

options.explanation: Birds is the subject, not the action.
Sing is the verb showing the action performed by the birds.
Beautifully is an adverb describing how the birds sing.
Birds sing is the subject and verb but not just the action alone.

questions.explanation: The verb in a sentence shows the action or state of being.
questions.hint: The action word is the verb in the sentence.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of these options contains a subject and a verb, making it a simple clause?

options.explanation: Running fast is a phrase as it lacks a subject.
Under the table is a phrase as it lacks a subject and verb.
She reads has a subject (She) and a verb (reads), forming a simple clause.
With great joy is a phrase as it lacks a subject and verb.

questions.explanation: A simple clause must have both a subject and a verb.
questions.hint: Look for a group of words that includes who or what (subject) and an action (verb).
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Consider the two parts of a statement: Assertion (A): Every complete sentence is a clause. Reason (R): A complete sentence always has a subject and a verb. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation for A.
options.explanation: Every complete sentence is a clause because it has a subject and a verb, and R correctly explains why.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation for A.
options.explanation: R is the correct explanation for A.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: R is true as a complete sentence must have a subject and a verb.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: A is true because every complete sentence is a clause.

questions.explanation: Every complete sentence must have a subject and a verb, which defines a clause.
questions.hint: A complete sentence is a clause because it contains a subject and a verb.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Identify the words that form a complete 'clause' in the following sentence: 'My brother plays football every evening.'

options.explanation: Every evening is a phrase as it lacks a subject and verb.
Plays football is the predicate but lacks the subject.
My brother plays football includes the subject (My brother) and the verb (plays), forming a complete clause.
My brother is only the subject, not a complete clause.

questions.explanation: A clause must contain a subject and a verb to express a complete thought.
questions.hint: Look for the group of words that includes the subject and the main verb.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences has *two* groups of words, each with its own subject and verb?

options.text: The sun shines brightly in the sky.
options.explanation: This sentence has only one subject-verb pair.

options.text: My friend and I went to the park.
options.explanation: This sentence has one subject (My friend and I) and one verb (went).

options.text: The dog barked, and the cat ran away.
options.explanation: This sentence has two clauses: 'The dog barked' and 'the cat ran away', each with its own subject and verb.

options.text: She is reading a very interesting book.
options.explanation: This sentence has one subject-verb pair.

questions.explanation: A sentence with two clauses will have two separate subject-verb pairs.
questions.hint: Look for a sentence with two independent clauses joined by a conjunction like 'and' or 'but'.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Read the short story below: 'The little bird built a nest. It laid three eggs. Soon, baby birds hatched.' How many groups of words (clauses) in these sentences contain a subject and a verb, each telling a complete thought?

options.explanation: There are more than one clauses in the sentences.
There are three clauses in the sentences.
Each sentence has one clause: 'The little bird built a nest', 'It laid three eggs', and 'Soon, baby birds hatched'.
There are only three clauses in the sentences.

questions.explanation: Each sentence in the story contains one clause with a subject and a verb.
questions.hint: Count the number of independent clauses in the given sentences.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: What are the two fundamental components of a clause?

options.explanation: A noun and adjective do not form the core of a clause.
Adverbs and prepositions are parts of speech but not the core components of a clause.
A clause must have a subject and a verb to express a complete thought.
A phrase is a group of words without a subject and verb, and a sentence is a complete thought.

questions.explanation: A clause must contain a subject (who or what is doing the action) and a verb (the action or state of being).
questions.hint: Think about what makes a clause complete.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: In the sentence 'When the bell rings, students go home,' which part is a group of words that has a subject and a verb but does NOT express a complete thought on its own?

options.explanation: This part expresses a complete thought.
This is just a verb phrase and does not express a complete thought.
This part has a subject and verb but does not express a complete thought on its own.
This is just a noun phrase and does not have a verb.

questions.explanation: 'When the bell rings' has a subject ('the bell') and a verb ('rings'), but it starts with 'When' and leaves you waiting for more information, so it does not express a complete thought on its own.
questions.hint: Look for the part that introduces a condition but does not finish the idea.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of these is a complete sentence?

options.explanation: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence as it lacks a subject and a verb.
This is a complete sentence with a subject ('the dog') and a verb ('barks').
This is a phrase, not a complete sentence as it lacks a subject and a verb.
This is a phrase, not a complete sentence as it lacks a subject and a verb.

questions.explanation: A complete sentence must have a subject (the dog) and a verb (barks) to express a full thought. Options A, C, and D are phrases, not complete sentences.
questions.hint: Look for a group of words that expresses a complete thought with a subject and a verb.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: In the sentence 'The birds sing sweetly,' what is the action word?

options.explanation: This is an article, not an action word.
This is the subject, not the action word.
This is the action word or verb in the sentence.
This is an adverb describing how the birds sing, not the action word itself.

questions.explanation: The action word, or verb, tells us what the subject is doing. In this sentence, 'sing' is the action performed by the birds.
questions.hint: Identify the word that describes what the birds are doing.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: What must a group of words have to be called a complete idea or sentence part?

options.explanation: A noun alone does not express a complete idea.
A verb alone does not express a complete idea.

options.text: Both a subject and a verb
options.explanation: A complete idea requires both a subject and a verb.
A describing word alone does not express a complete idea.

questions.explanation: For a group of words to express a complete idea (which is the essence of a simple clause or sentence), it needs both a subject (who or what is doing the action) and a verb (the action itself).
questions.hint: Think about what makes a sentence complete.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Look at the sentence: 'My sister reads a book.' Which part tells us WHO is doing the action?

options.explanation: This is a possessive pronoun, not the subject performing the action.
This is the subject performing the action (reading).
This is the verb, not the subject performing the action.
This is the object receiving the action, not the subject performing it.

questions.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the person or thing performing the action. Here, 'sister' is the one who is reading.

questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Read the sentence: 'The sun shines, and the flowers bloom.' How many parts of this sentence have their own action word (verb)?

options.explanation: The sentence has more than one part with a subject and a verb.
There are two parts: 'The sun shines' and 'the flowers bloom'.
The sentence does not have three parts with subjects and verbs.
The sentence clearly has parts with subjects and verbs.

questions.explanation: The sentence can be broken into two parts, each with its own subject and verb: 'The sun shines' (sun is subject, shines is verb) and 'the flowers bloom' (flowers is subject, bloom is verb). These two parts are joined by 'and'.
questions.hint: Count the number of independent clauses or parts with a subject and a verb.

questions.question: Which of these groups of words is NOT a complete idea (does not have both a subject and a verb)?

options.explanation: This is a complete sentence with a subject ('my friend') and a verb ('plays').
This is a complete sentence with a subject ('the cat') and a verb ('slept').
This is a phrase, not a complete sentence as it lacks a subject and a verb.

questions.question: Fill in the blank to connect these two complete ideas: 'I like mangoes ______ my brother likes bananas.'

options.explanation: 'But' implies contrast, which does not fit the context of liking similar fruits.
'With' implies accompaniment, which does not fit the context of liking different fruits.

questions.hint: Choose the conjunction that best connects two similar ideas.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Assertion (A): 'He smiled' is a complete sentence. Reason (R): It has a subject ('He') and a verb ('smiled').

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation for A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains why 'He smiled' is a complete sentence.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation for A.
options.explanation: The reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.

questions.explanation: 'He smiled' is indeed a complete sentence. The reason it is complete is precisely because it contains both a subject ('He') and a verb ('smiled'), which forms a complete thought (or a simple independent clause).

questions.question: Read the passage: 'The little bird sang a sweet song. It flew high in the sky. Then, it landed on a tree branch.' How many separate complete action parts (groups of words with a subject and a verb) are there in this passage?

options.explanation: There are more than one complete action parts in the passage.
There are three complete action parts in the passage.
There are three complete action parts: 'The little bird sang a sweet song,' 'It flew high in the sky,' and 'Then, it landed on a tree branch.'
There are only three complete action parts in the passage.

questions.explanation: Each sentence in the passage is a separate complete action part, which is essentially a simple clause. 1. 'The little bird sang a sweet song.' (Subject: bird, Verb: sang) 2. 'It flew high in the sky.' (Subject: it, Verb: flew) 3. 'Then, it landed on a tree branch.' (Subject: it, Verb: landed)
questions.hint: Count the number of sentences or independent clauses in the passage.

questions.question: What is the subject in the sentence 'It flew high in the sky'?

options.explanation: Sky is the object of the preposition 'in', not the subject.
Correct. 'It' is the subject performing the action 'flew'.
'Flew' is the verb, not the subject.
'High' is an adverb describing how the action was performed.

questions.question: What is the verb in the sentence 'it landed on a tree branch'?

options.explanation: 'It' is the subject, not the verb.

questions.question: How many distinct complete action parts are present in the given sentences?

options.explanation: There are two sentences, each with one complete action part.
Correct. Each sentence has one complete action part: 'It flew' and 'it landed'.
There are only two sentences provided.
There are only two sentences provided.

questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences contains two complete ideas joined together?

options.text: My mother cooks delicious food for us.
options.explanation: This is a single independent clause with one complete idea.

options.text: The cat chased the mouse quickly.
options.explanation: This is a single independent clause with one complete idea.

options.text: I play football, but my friend plays basketball.
options.explanation: Correct. This sentence has two independent clauses joined by 'but'.

options.text: After school, we go home happily.
options.explanation: This is a single independent clause with one complete idea.

questions.explanation: A sentence with two complete ideas joined together contains two independent clauses connected by a conjunction. Option C, 'I play football, but my friend plays basketball,' has two independent clauses joined by 'but'.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences contains a **noun clause**?

options.explanation: This is a simple sentence with no clause.
The clause 'where she lives' acts as the object of the verb 'know'.
This is a simple sentence with no clause.
This is a simple sentence with no clause.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'I know where she lives' contains a noun clause 'where she lives' functioning as the object of the verb 'know.' Noun clauses begin with words like *where, what, how,* or *that.*

questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Identify the **adjective clause** in the following sentence: 'The book that you gave me is interesting.'

options.explanation: This is the noun being modified, not the clause.
This clause modifies 'book' and starts with 'that.'
This is the predicate, not a clause.

questions.explanation: 'that you gave me' is an adjective clause modifying the noun 'book.' Adjective clauses typically begin with *who, which, that,* or *whose.*

questions.question: Which sentence uses a **relative pronoun** correctly?

options.text: This is the man who helped me.

questions.question: Read the sentence carefully: 'The place where I was born is very beautiful.' The underlined part is a/an:

options.explanation: This clause modifies a verb, not an adjective.
This clause does not describe a noun.

questions.question: Which of the following is **NOT** a type of subordinate clause?

options.explanation: This is a type of subordinate clause.
This is a type of subordinate clause.
This is an independent clause, not a subordinate clause.

options.explanation: Both A and R are true.

questions.question: Choose the correct clause to complete the sentence: '_____ is surprising.'

options.explanation: This noun clause acts as the subject.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a **contrast** adverb clause?

options.text: Although she was tired, she finished her work.

options.text: A group of words that contains a subject and a verb.
options.explanation: This is the correct definition of a clause.

options.text: A single word that describes an action.
options.explanation: This describes a verb, not a clause.

questions.explanation: A clause is defined as a group of words that has both a subject and a verb. It may or may not make complete sense on its own (depending on if it's an independent or dependent clause).
questions.hint: A clause must contain a subject and a verb.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Identify the clause in the following sentence: 'The cat slept.'

options.explanation: This is a phrase, not a clause, as it lacks a verb.
This is a verb, not a clause, as it lacks a subject.
This is a clause with a subject ('The cat') and a verb ('slept').
This is a single word, not a clause.

questions.explanation: 'The cat slept' is a clause because it has a subject ('The cat') and a verb ('slept'). It also forms a complete thought.
questions.hint: Look for a group of words with a subject and a verb.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: In the sentence, 'My mother cooks delicious food,' which part is the main clause?

options.explanation: This is a phrase, not a clause.
This is the main clause as it contains a subject and verb and forms a complete sentence.
This is a phrase, not a clause, as it lacks a subject.
This is a phrase, not a clause, as it lacks a verb.

questions.explanation: A main clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence. 'My mother cooks delicious food' contains the subject 'My mother' and the verb 'cooks' and expresses a complete thought.
questions.hint: A main clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Choose the option that is a dependent (subordinate) clause.

options.explanation: This is an independent clause as it can stand alone.
This is an independent clause as it can stand alone.
This is a dependent clause as it starts with 'because' and cannot stand alone.
This is an independent clause as it can stand alone.

questions.explanation: A dependent clause has a subject ('it') and a verb ('was raining') but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence because of the subordinating conjunction 'because' at the beginning. It needs to be attached to a main clause to make complete sense.
questions.hint: A dependent clause often starts with a subordinating conjunction like 'because,' 'if,' or 'although.'
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Complete the sentence with an appropriate clause: 'I will play outside ______.'

options.explanation: This is a phrase, not a clause.
This is a phrase, not a clause.
This is a dependent clause with a subject ('the weather') and a verb ('is').
This is a phrase, not a clause.

questions.explanation: The sentence requires a clause to complete the condition. 'if the weather is good' is a dependent clause that provides the condition for playing outside, containing a subject ('the weather') and a verb ('is'). Options A, B, and D are phrases, not clauses.
questions.hint: Look for a group of words that includes a subject and a verb to complete the sentence logically.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a dependent clause to add more information?

options.text: The boy ran quickly and jumped high.
options.explanation: This combines two phrases with a conjunction, not a dependent clause.

options.text: She likes to read books and watch movies.
options.explanation: This combines two phrases with a conjunction, not a dependent clause.

options.text: My friend, who lives next door, has a new bicycle.
options.explanation: This sentence uses the dependent clause 'who lives next door' to add information about 'My friend.'

options.text: We visited the zoo, then we ate lunch.
options.explanation: This combines two independent clauses with a conjunction, not a dependent clause.

questions.explanation: 'who lives next door' is a dependent (relative) clause that provides extra information about 'My friend.' It contains a subject ('who' referring to friend) and a verb ('lives') but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Options A, B, and D either use phrases or combine two independent clauses without a dependent clause.
questions.hint: A dependent clause often provides additional information and cannot stand alone.
questions.subject: upbo5-english

questions.question: Read the following sentence: 'Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.' Identify the main clause and the dependent clause in this sentence.

options.text: Main Clause: Although it was raining | Dependent Clause: we decided to go for a walk
options.explanation: The main clause and dependent clause are reversed.

options.text: Main Clause: we decided | Dependent Clause: to go for a walk
options.explanation: This incorrectly splits the main clause into two parts.

options.text: Main Clause: we decided to go for a walk | Dependent Clause: Although it was raining
options.explanation: This correctly identifies the main clause and dependent clause.

options.text: Main Clause: it was raining | Dependent Clause: we decided to go for a walk
options.explanation: The main clause and dependent clause are reversed.

questions.explanation: The main clause is 'we decided to go for a walk' because it can stand alone as a complete sentence. The dependent clause is 'Although it was raining' because it starts with the subordinating conjunction 'Although' and cannot stand alone, needing the main clause to make complete sense.
questions.hint: The main clause can stand alone, while the dependent clause cannot.
questions.subject: upbo5-english
